segments.name: Families with Children
segments.description: Households with school-aged children balancing work, school pickups, and complex dietary preferences or refusals.
needs: Quick weeknight recipes under thirty minutes
Accommodating children's preferences and food refusals
Reducing food waste and grocery overspending

segments.name: Couples Without Children
segments.description: Couples ranging from busy working professionals with erratic schedules (P02, P05, P08) to retired couples with established routines (P09).
needs: Low-effort setup that avoids manual pantry entry
Flexibility for impromptu dining or schedule changes

segments.name: Shared Households / Flatmates
segments.description: Multiple flatmates sharing a single kitchen with decentralized cooking habits and coordination challenges.
needs: Shared visibility of pantry and grocery needs
Clear tracking of shared vs individual items

segments.name: Single Households
segments.description: Individuals living alone who predominantly eat out, order delivery, or cook minimal single-portion meals without planning.
needs: Small-portion sizing or minimal-effort cooking options

insights.statement: Food waste and forgotten items expiring at the back of the fridge are widespread pain points.

evidence.quote: Things disappear in the back of the fridge and I find them two weeks later, usually when they're already off.
We throw away so much food. Half a cucumber, wilted herbs, yoghurt that expired last week.
The waste bothers me, both the money and the guilt. I probably lose twenty or thirty euros a week.
I buy vegetables with good intentions and then bin them on Sunday.
Things disappear in the back of the fridge and I find them two weeks later, usually when they're already off.
Nobody remembers what we already have, so we buy duplicates and then one of them goes bad.

caveats: Financial losses from waste are stated estimates.

insights.statement: Daily decision fatigue regarding what to cook on weeknights causes stress and friction.

evidence.quote: Every single day somebody has to decide what's for dinner, and that somebody is me.
We both get home late, so it's usually pasta or something quick. We would like more variety but it never happens.
Deciding is exhausting. I would rather cook anything than think about what to cook.
The worst part is the daily question of what to cook. By Wednesday I have no ideas left.
Around four in the afternoon the 'what do we eat tonight' dread starts.
It's chaos between school pickups, homework and work calls. Dinner is whatever I can get on the table in thirty minutes.

caveats: P03 exhibited internal contradiction between liking Sunday planning and finding deciding exhausting.

insights.statement: Setup must be extremely fast and low-effort to prevent user churn.

evidence.quote: Setup has to be fast. If I need to type in my whole pantry I'll quit on day two.

caveats: Heavy reliance on templated phrasing across multiple interviews indicates potential probing bias by the interviewer.

insights.statement: Users vary significantly in shopping rhythm between structured weekly trips and daily top-ups.

evidence.quote: I shop once a week, usually on Saturday, plus a couple of top-up trips.
I shop once a week, usually on Saturday, plus a couple of top-up trips.
I go to the shop almost every day and buy as I go.
I go to the shop almost every day and buy as I go.

caveats: A weekly meal plan with a weekly shopping list aligns best with weekly shoppers, whereas daily shoppers require different workflows.

disagreements.topic: Value of meal planning and structure versus spontaneous cooking

positions.stance: Planning ahead is enjoyable, structured, and essential for budget and control.

evidence.quote: Planning is my favourite part of the week, honestly. I would never want an app to take that away from me.

positions.stance: Planning ahead causes stress, and strict plans feel like failure when deviated from.

evidence.quote: Planning ahead stresses me out. A plan I don't follow feels like failure, so I decide on the day.

disagreements.implication: PantryPal must accommodate both structured planners and spontaneous cooks by offering flexible plans that can be easily modified without making users feel like they failed.

disagreements.topic: Trust in automated recommendations versus manual control

positions.stance: Open to app assistance provided the user retains full editing control and flexibility.

evidence.quote: I want to edit the plan easily. I don't want an app dictating to me.

positions.stance: Distrustful of automated apps dictating habits; prefer simple, private, or manual methods.

evidence.quote: I don't trust apps with my shopping habits, so it would have to be very simple and private.

disagreements.implication: The product messaging and UI must emphasize user agency, easy editing, and privacy rather than algorithmic imposition.

willingness_to_pay: Willingness to pay typically ranges from a few euros up to 5-6 euros per month, conditional on the app clearly saving money on groceries or reducing food waste. Several participants (P05, P07, P09) state they would not pay and require a free version with ads. An outlier (P08) stated 30 euros per month, which is excluded from typical figures as it was anchored on a catastrophic holiday fridge disaster rather than normal weekly planning.

willingness_to_pay_evidence.quote: A few euros a month, maybe, if it clearly saves me money on groceries.
Maybe five or six euros. More than that and I'd just keep my notes app.
A few euros a month, maybe, if it clearly saves me money on groceries.
A few euros a month, maybe, if it clearly saves me money on groceries.
Honestly I wouldn't pay for it. I'd want a free version.
Honestly I wouldn't pay for it. I'd want a free version.
For something that would stop that, I'd pay thirty euros a month, easy.

evidence_set_aside: P06 excluded entirely due to major leading interview issues and verbatim copying of P01.
P08 willingness to pay of EUR 30/month excluded from typical figures as an outlier anchored on a holiday incident rather than weekly dinner planning.
P03 internal contradiction regarding meal planning (calling planning the favourite part of the week vs. calling deciding exhausting) requires cautious interpretation.
P04 attribution inconsistency (switching between wife and husband) requires cautious attribution.
